screens.title: Collision Detection and Triggers
screens.narratorSegment: Collision detection is one of the core systems you will use to make your game world respond to the player and other objects. In Unity this system is built on two complementary building blocks: colliders, which define invisible physical boundaries, and rigidbodies, which allow objects to be moved by the physics engine. You will learn the practical difference between collisions that physically block or bounce objects, and triggers that detect overlaps without blocking movement. The chapter walks you through concrete C# examples for collecting a coin with a trigger and taking damage from a hazard with a collision. You will also learn how Physics Layers can prevent unwanted interactions and improve performance. By the end, you should be able to decide when to use a MeshCollider versus a primitive collider, which object needs a Rigidbody, and how to wire up OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter to respond to gameplay events. Think about a doorway versus a wall: one detects you passing through, the other stops you. That analogy will help as you build scenes and scripts.

screens.title: What is a Collider?
screens.narratorSegment: A Collider is an invisible geometric shape attached to a GameObject that tells Unity where the object exists for the physics engine. Primitive colliders like BoxCollider, SphereCollider, and CapsuleCollider are fast because they use simple math; they should be your first choice for moving objects like players, bullets, and pickups. MeshCollider uses the object's mesh and can precisely match complex visuals, but it is more computationally expensive and usually best for static environment geometry. Importantly, a Collider by itself does not automatically let an object be moved by physics; that requires a Rigidbody. If a GameObject has only a Collider and no Rigidbody it is treated as a static collider: it can block Rigidbody objects but will not respond to physics forces. Concrete example: a floor with only a BoxCollider will stop a falling rigidbody player, while a moving enemy that should be pushed must have both a collider and a Rigidbody. A common misconception is equating having a Collider with being physically dynamic; remember that Rigidbody is the component that gives physics motion. Takeaway: pick primitive colliders when possible for better performance and reserve MeshColliders for static complex geometry.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is a Collider?
Definition

A Collider is a component that defines an invisible shape used by Unity's physics to detect contact and overlap with other objects.

Box / Sphere / Capsule
Fast primitive shapes for most moving objects.
MeshCollider
Accurate but expensive; prefer for static complex geometry.
Common mistake
Assuming a Collider alone makes an object dynamic. Without a Rigidbody the object stays static for physics simulation.
Concrete example

A level's rock pile can use MeshColliders for accuracy if it never moves. A player capsule should use a CapsuleCollider for cheap, stable collision checks while moving.

Why it matters
  • Performance: primitives are far cheaper than mesh collisions.
  • Correctness: colliders determine contact points and overlap detection.
  • Gameplay: collider size affects what the player can reach and what triggers fire.
Key Takeaway

Choose primitive colliders for moving objects; use MeshCollider only for static complex shapes.

screens.title: Rigidbody and Static Colliders
screens.narratorSegment: The Rigidbody component is what tells Unity an object should be part of the physics simulation. A Rigidbody receives forces, gravity, and impulse from collisions and enables events like OnCollisionEnter to be generated. When a Rigidbody collides with a static collider — one that has a Collider but no Rigidbody — the Rigidbody will react and the static collider remains unmoved. If both objects have Rigidbodies, both will respond according to mass and applied forces. There is a useful middle ground called Is Kinematic: a kinematic Rigidbody is not moved by physics forces but can still generate collision and trigger events and influence other rigidbodies when moved by script. A common confusion is when neither object has a Rigidbody: they can visually intersect or block each other in the editor, but Unity will not fire collision or trigger callbacks because the physics engine only tracks contacts between at least one Rigidbody. Example: a moving projectile should have a Rigidbody to generate OnCollisionEnter, while a decorative wall intended only to block movement may have a Collider only and no Rigidbody. Takeaway: add a Rigidbody to the object that should be detected or moved; use kinematic Rigidbody for scripted motion that still needs to communicate with physics.

keyIdea.title: Rigidbody rule
keyIdea.text: At least one interacting object must have a Rigidbody for OnCollision or OnTrigger events to fire; Is Kinematic enables scripted motion while still generating events.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Rigidbody and Static Colliders
What a Rigidbody does
  • Enables gravity and force-based motion.
  • Generates collision/trigger events with colliders.
  • Interacts with other Rigidbodies according to mass and forces.
Static Collider behavior

A Collider without a Rigidbody is static for physics: it blocks Rigidbody objects but is not moved by them.

Note: Is Kinematic turns off physics-driven motion but still allows event generation and scripted movement.
Concrete scenario

Your projectile should carry a Rigidbody so when it hits a destructible wall the OnCollisionEnter message happens. If the wall has no Rigidbody, consider adding a kinematic Rigidbody if you need it to detect collisions in code without being physically pushed.

Key Takeaway

Make sure at least one object has a Rigidbody to trigger collision or trigger events. Use kinematic for scripted movers.

screens.title: Trigger example: Coin script
screens.narratorSegment: Triggers detect overlaps without causing a physical response. The typical pattern is to mark a collider as Is Trigger and then implement OnTriggerEnter in a script attached to the trigger object. In the coin example the Coin script listens for OnTriggerEnter and checks that the object entering has the Player tag before destroying itself and optionally adding score. This keeps collection logic simple and avoids physical blocking. An important detail: for the trigger to call OnTriggerEnter at least one of the two objects involved must have a Rigidbody. Usually the player has a Rigidbody and the coin is a static trigger. A common misconception is thinking triggers will fire between two static colliders; they will not. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Coin Trigger Script
Usage pattern

A trigger detects overlap and passes a Collider reference to your script. Common use cases are pickups, zone entry, or area activation where you do not want the objects to block each other.

Important
At least one of the colliding objects must have a Rigidbody for OnTriggerEnter to fire.
C# example
using UnityEngine;

public class Coin : MonoBehaviour
{
  public int coinValue = 1; // How many points this coin is worth

  void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
  {
    // Check if the object entering the trigger is the Player
    if (other.CompareTag("Player"))
    {
      Debug.Log("Player collected a coin!");
      // In a real game, you'd add to score, play sound, etc.
      Destroy(gameObject);
    }
  }
}
Copy this into a Coin script and attach it to a trigger collider. Make sure the Player has a Rigidbody and is tagged "Player".

The typical method is OnCollisionEnter which receives a Collision object containing contact points and relative velocity. In the SpikeHazard example, the Hazard script checks whether the colliding object is the Player using CompareTag and then logs or deducts health. This pattern is ideal for hazards, bullets hitting destructibles, or any situation where you want a physical reaction. A common pitfall is placing OnCollisionEnter only on a static wall that lacks a Rigidbody; if the moving object has the Rigidbody, prefer placing the logic on either object, but remember at least one Rigidbody is required. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Hazard Collision Script
When to use collision

Choose collisions when objects should physically interact or bounce. Collisions give you rich data like contact points that are helpful for impact effects.

Misconception
If you don’t see OnCollisionEnter firing, check whether both objects are colliders only. At least one needs a Rigidbody.
C# example
using UnityEngine;

public class Hazard : MonoBehaviour
{
  public int damageAmount = 10; // How much damage this hazard deals

  void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
  {
    // Check if the object colliding with the hazard is the Player
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player"))
    {
      Debug.Log("Player collided with a hazard! Took " + damageAmount + " damage.");
      // In a real game, subtract health, play sound, etc.
    }
  }
}
Attach to a non-trigger collider on the hazard. Confirm the Player has a Rigidbody so this callback fires.

screens.title: Collision vs Trigger
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between collisions and triggers is essential to choosing the correct behavior for game objects. Collisions physically block or bounce objects and provide Collision data; they are used when two objects should not pass through one another, like a player hitting a wall or a bullet impacting an enemy. Triggers, by contrast, detect overlaps without causing a physical response and supply Collider data; they are perfect for pickups, area-based effects, and entering zones that start scripted events. A helpful real-world contrast: a wall is a collision — you stop when you hit it. A doorway sensor is a trigger — you step through and the sensor notices you without stopping you. Remember the technical rule: for either OnCollision or OnTrigger events to fire at least one involved GameObject must have a Rigidbody. A common error is marking a collider as a trigger but forgetting the Rigidbody on both objects; nothing will fire. When designing your scene, decide whether you want physics response or only detection, then set Is Trigger appropriately and ensure Rigidbody presence. Closing question: for a healing potion that should disappear and restore health when the player passes through it, would you use a collision or trigger? (Use a trigger.)

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Collision vs Trigger
Collision
  • Physical blocking and bounce.
  • Provides Collision data (contacts, relative velocity).
  • Use for walls, hazards, stacking objects.
Requires: colliders not marked as Trigger; at least one Rigidbody.
Trigger
  • Detects overlap without blocking.
  • Provides Collider data (which collider entered).
  • Use for pickups, zones, and detection ranges.
Requires: collider marked Is Trigger; at least one Rigidbody.
Example decision

A coin should be a trigger so the player passes through and the coin disappears. A spike should be a collision so the player physically collides and can be stopped or bounce.

screens.title: Using Tags and CompareTag
screens.narratorSegment: Tags are a lightweight way to identify GameObjects at runtime. The chapter recommends using CompareTag inside OnCollisionEnter or OnTriggerEnter instead of comparing strings directly to reduce overhead and avoid typo mistakes. For example, in both the Coin and Hazard scripts we check whether the other collider belongs to the Player using CompareTag("Player"). This ensures our response code only runs when the player interacts, not when other objects disturb the trigger or collider. A common mistake is using name comparisons or relying on layers alone for identity; layers are better for broad filtering while tags are good for specific role checks. When designing your scene, tag the player and any special interactors early so your scripts can remain simple and defensive. Also, keep tags consistent: if you create a new Player prefab, verify its tag so CompareTag calls still succeed. Takeaway: prefer CompareTag for fast, clear identity checks in collision and trigger handlers. screens.title: Physics Layers and Collision Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: Physics Layers let you control which categories of objects can collide or trigger with one another. In Unity’s Project Settings under Physics you will find the Collision Matrix, a grid where you can uncheck boxes to prevent interactions between specific layers. This is powerful for preventing unwanted interactions, such as player bullets colliding with the player’s own collider, or UI elements interfering with world physics. Using layers reduces unnecessary physics checks and therefore improves performance, especially in scenes with many objects. A practical workflow is to define layers for Player, Enemy, Projectile, Environment, and UI, then disable collisions that are not needed. Remember that layer filtering affects both collision and trigger checks, so if you disable collision between two layers you will also prevent trigger events between them. A common misconception is thinking tags are sufficient for filtering — tags are for identity checks inside code; layers control the physics engine’s pairwise checks. Takeaway: configure the collision matrix early to avoid wasted physics cycles and to enforce intended gameplay interactions. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Physics Layers
Why layers matter

Layers let the physics engine skip unnecessary pairwise checks and prevent unwanted interactions. This is especially useful in larger scenes with many colliders.

Example layers: Player, Enemy, Projectile, Environment, UI. Disable collisions between Projectile and Player if bullets should not hit the shooter.
How to configure
  1. Open Project Settings → Physics.
  2. In the Collision Matrix, uncheck pairs that should not interact.
  3. Test in play mode to confirm expected callbacks still occur.

fullNarratorScript:
Collision detection is one of the core systems you will use to make your game world respond to the player and other objects. In Unity this system is built on two complementary building blocks: colliders, which define invisible physical boundaries, and rigidbodies, which allow objects to be moved by the physics engine. You will learn the practical difference between collisions that physically block or bounce objects, and triggers that detect overlaps without blocking movement. The chapter walks you through concrete C# examples for collecting a coin with a trigger and taking damage from a hazard with a collision. You will also learn how Physics Layers can prevent unwanted interactions and improve performance. By the end, you should be able to decide when to use a MeshCollider versus a primitive collider, which object needs a Rigidbody, and how to wire up OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter to respond to gameplay events. Think about a doorway versus a wall: one detects you passing through, the other stops you. That analogy will help as you build scenes and scripts.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use in a Unity scene. First, you will tell the difference between a Collider and the role it plays in physics interactions compared to a Rigidbody that enables movement and response. Second, you will explain how collision events such as OnCollisionEnter differ from trigger events like OnTriggerEnter, including what data each provides to your scripts. Third, you will implement small C# scripts that detect and respond to collisions and triggers, using concrete examples like collecting a coin or taking damage from a hazard. Finally, you will configure Physics Layers and the collision matrix so only intended objects interact, improving both correctness and performance. Each objective includes a short rationale and a small mnemonic to help you remember when to use the feature. Practically, after this module you should be able to set up a collectible trigger, a physical hazard, tag objects correctly, and verify the collision matrix so gameplay behaves as expected.

This lesson includes a hands-on lab where you will create a collectible coin that uses a trigger, and a spike hazard that uses a physical collision. The practice begins by adding colliders and confirming the Is Trigger checkbox for the coin, then attaching a Coin script that detects OnTriggerEnter and destroys the coin. For the hazard, add a BoxCollider without Is Trigger checked and a Hazard script that handles OnCollisionEnter to log damage. Tag your Player object and use CompareTag in scripts to ensure only the intended object triggers events. Finally, test the interaction and inspect logs to confirm the correct callbacks fired. These practice steps reinforce the conceptual differences and help you detect common misconfigurations like missing rigidbodies or mis-tagged objects. The lab ends with a checkpoint: verify the coin disappears on contact and the hazard logs a collision message when hit.

A Collider is an invisible geometric shape attached to a GameObject that tells Unity where the object exists for the physics engine. Primitive colliders like BoxCollider, SphereCollider, and CapsuleCollider are fast because they use simple math; they should be your first choice for moving objects like players, bullets, and pickups. MeshCollider uses the object's mesh and can precisely match complex visuals, but it is more computationally expensive and usually best for static environment geometry. Importantly, a Collider by itself does not automatically let an object be moved by physics; that requires a Rigidbody. If a GameObject has only a Collider and no Rigidbody it is treated as a static collider: it can block Rigidbody objects but will not respond to physics forces. Concrete example: a floor with only a BoxCollider will stop a falling rigidbody player, while a moving enemy that should be pushed must have both a collider and a Rigidbody. A common misconception is equating having a Collider with being physically dynamic; remember that Rigidbody is the component that gives physics motion. Takeaway: pick primitive colliders when possible for better performance and reserve MeshColliders for static complex geometry.

The Rigidbody component is what tells Unity an object should be part of the physics simulation. A Rigidbody receives forces, gravity, and impulse from collisions and enables events like OnCollisionEnter to be generated. When a Rigidbody collides with a static collider — one that has a Collider but no Rigidbody — the Rigidbody will react and the static collider remains unmoved. If both objects have Rigidbodies, both will respond according to mass and applied forces. There is a useful middle ground called Is Kinematic: a kinematic Rigidbody is not moved by physics forces but can still generate collision and trigger events and influence other rigidbodies when moved by script. A common confusion is when neither object has a Rigidbody: they can visually intersect or block each other in the editor, but Unity will not fire collision or trigger callbacks because the physics engine only tracks contacts between at least one Rigidbody. Example: a moving projectile should have a Rigidbody to generate OnCollisionEnter, while a decorative wall intended only to block movement may have a Collider only and no Rigidbody. Takeaway: add a Rigidbody to the object that should be detected or moved; use kinematic Rigidbody for scripted motion that still needs to communicate with physics.

Triggers detect overlaps without causing a physical response. The typical pattern is to mark a collider as Is Trigger and then implement OnTriggerEnter in a script attached to the trigger object. In the coin example the Coin script listens for OnTriggerEnter and checks that the object entering has the Player tag before destroying itself and optionally adding score. This keeps collection logic simple and avoids physical blocking. An important detail: for the trigger to call OnTriggerEnter at least one of the two objects involved must have a Rigidbody. Usually the player has a Rigidbody and the coin is a static trigger. A common misconception is thinking triggers will fire between two static colliders; they will not. Below is the exact C# structure used in the chapter so you can copy it into your Unity project and test the coin disappearing on contact. After you try it, ask yourself whether the player or the object should carry the Rigidbody and why. Trigger example: Coin script means mark a collider as is trigger and use ontriggerenter to detect overlaps; ensure at least one object has a rigidbody.. In practical terms, ontriggerenter used to detect and collect items without blocking movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Collisions represent physical impacts where objects cannot pass through each other. To receive collision callbacks, at least one object involved must have a Rigidbody and colliders must not be marked as triggers. The typical method is OnCollisionEnter which receives a Collision object containing contact points and relative velocity. In the SpikeHazard example, the Hazard script checks whether the colliding object is the Player using CompareTag and then logs or deducts health. This pattern is ideal for hazards, bullets hitting destructibles, or any situation where you want a physical reaction. A common pitfall is placing OnCollisionEnter only on a static wall that lacks a Rigidbody; if the moving object has the Rigidbody, prefer placing the logic on either object, but remember at least one Rigidbody is required. Below is the Hazard script from the chapter to replicate the behavior and observe the console when the player collides. Collision example: Hazard script means use oncollisionenter for physical impacts; ensure colliders are not triggers and at least one object has a rigidbody.. In practical terms, using oncollisionenter to respond to physical impacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the difference between collisions and triggers is essential to choosing the correct behavior for game objects. Collisions physically block or bounce objects and provide Collision data; they are used when two objects should not pass through one another, like a player hitting a wall or a bullet impacting an enemy. Triggers, by contrast, detect overlaps without causing a physical response and supply Collider data; they are perfect for pickups, area-based effects, and entering zones that start scripted events. A helpful real-world contrast: a wall is a collision — you stop when you hit it. A doorway sensor is a trigger — you step through and the sensor notices you without stopping you. Remember the technical rule: for either OnCollision or OnTrigger events to fire at least one involved GameObject must have a Rigidbody. A common error is marking a collider as a trigger but forgetting the Rigidbody on both objects; nothing will fire. When designing your scene, decide whether you want physics response or only detection, then set Is Trigger appropriately and ensure Rigidbody presence. Closing question: for a healing potion that should disappear and restore health when the player passes through it, would you use a collision or trigger? (Use a trigger.)

This ensures the player can both move and fire physics callbacks. Step two: create a Sphere named Coin, add or confirm it has a Collider, and check Is Trigger in the Inspector. Attach the Hazard script and set damageAmount. Step four: run the scene and observe console messages when interactions occur. If the coin doesn't disappear or the hazard doesn't log, verify tags and Rigidbody presence. Step five: iterate — adjust collider sizes so the visual shape matches gameplay expectations. MeshCollider provides a precise collision shape by using a mesh, but it is more computationally expensive compared to primitive colliders. The chapter emphasizes reserving MeshCollider for static environment geometry where the object does not move. For example, a detailed cave wall or large terrain piece that never changes can use a MeshCollider so collisions match the visuals exactly without the overhead of having it interact dynamically. For moving objects or many small objects, prefer combinations of primitives or compound colliders built from multiple primitive shapes. A frequent error is assigning MeshCollider to many moving objects, which can cause physics slowdowns. If you must use MeshCollider for a moving object, consider marking it Convex where appropriate and be aware of the trade-offs. Physics Layers let you control which categories of objects can collide or trigger with one another. In Unity’s Project Settings under Physics you will find the Collision Matrix, a grid where you can uncheck boxes to prevent interactions between specific layers. This is powerful for preventing unwanted interactions, such as player bullets colliding with the player’s own collider, or UI elements interfering with world physics. Using layers reduces unnecessary physics checks and therefore improves performance, especially in scenes with many objects. A practical workflow is to define layers for Player, Enemy, Projectile, Environment, and UI, then disable collisions that are not needed. Remember that layer filtering affects both collision and trigger checks, so if you disable collision between two layers you will also prevent trigger events between them. A common misconception is thinking tags are sufficient for filtering — tags are for identity checks inside code; layers control the physics engine’s pairwise checks.
